title: Occupation-condensation transition of a sublinearly vertex-reinforced random walk on regular tree
abstract: A vertex-reinforced random walk steps to a neighbour with probability proportional to $1+βn^{a}$, where $n$ counts previous visits to that neighbour and $a\in(0,1)$ sets the memory strength. On the rooted $b$-ary tree the exponential growth of the vertex set drives the walk outward while the reinforcement pulls it back. We report a sharp condensation transition of the occupation measure at a finite $β_c(a,b)$: below it the occupation spreads and the range grows linearly; above it a single vertex holds an $O(1)$ fraction of the time, stable in the observation time, while the range keeps growing very slowly, at a rate better described by $\log t$ than by any power. We do not find the range to be bounded, and keep this condensation distinct from finite-range localization. Four estimators locate the same threshold, which shows no systematic drift out to $t=3\times10^{7}$. In a frozen environment the walk is reversible, with edge conductances $c_{uv}=w_{u}w_{v}$, $w_{v}=1+βn_{v}^{a}$, and measure $μ_{v}\propto w_{v}\sum_{u\sim v}w_{u}$ describing the condensed core, whose neighbour coupling we test directly. Reversibility places the escape at the frontier within the branching-number criterion for biased walks on trees, predicting $β_c\propto b-1$; the measured lines for $b=2,3,4$ collapse under division by $b-1$ to a few percent (bootstrap). The value $a=1/2$ that governs the walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ enters only as the marginal exponent of the condensed profile. Near $β_c$ the occupancy is non-self-averaging and bimodal, a coexistence-type phenomenology.
summary: This work characterizes the occupation-condensation transition in a vertex-reinforced random walk on regular trees. The transition occurs at a critical reinforcement strength $\beta_c$, causing the walker's time spent to concentrate (condense) onto a small core set of vertices. This study uses scaling arguments and geometric constraints to map out this non-equilibrium phase boundary.
main_problem: The paper investigates the occupation-condensation transition of a sublinearly vertex-reinforced random walk (VRRW) on regular trees.
main_result: A sharp condensation transition exists at $\beta_c(a, b)$, where above this threshold, the walker's occupation concentrates on a few vertices while the overall range grows only logarithmically with time.
method: The analysis combines simulation studies of range exponents and condensate fractions with theoretical derivations based on reversible stationary measures for the core region.
model_or_system: The model is a VRRW on a rooted $b$-ary tree, where movement probability to a neighbor depends on previous visit counts via a sublinear reinforcement term ($1 + \beta n^a$).
key_observables: Range exponent ($\nu_R$), condensate fraction ($m_1$), and the transition line $\beta_c(a, b)$.
important_parameters: Memory strength $a \in (0, 1)$, reinforcement coupling $\beta$, and tree branching number $b$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on distinguishing between condensation and finite-range localization, and uses a 'frozen environment' approximation to determine the transition scaling law.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the range exponent crossing at $\beta_c$, show the collapse of the transition line $\beta_c/(b-1)$ for different $b$, and display the condensate fraction plateauing above threshold.
paper_structure:
The paper systematically analyzes the phase diagram by defining observables ($
u_R, m_1$), deriving theoretical predictions from reversible measures (the core), and confirming scaling laws ($\beta_c \propto b-1$) through data collapse across multiple geometries ($b=2, 3, 4$).
why_interesting: The study of non-equilibrium dynamics in geometrically constrained systems, like random walks on trees, provides a rich analogy for understanding energy/information localization or phase transitions in complex quantum many-body systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Condensation of the sublinear VRRW on the binary tree (b = 2). Left: range exponent νR in the (a, β) plane; νR = 1 (dark red) is linear spreading, small νR (dark blue) the condensed regime. Middle: transition line βc(a) from νR = 1/2, on a logarithmic β axis; βc decreases with a and rises steeply as a falls below ≈0.4. Right: condensate fraction m1 at t = 106 against β for several a; the rise marks the onset of condensation.

Figure 2: Occupation of the condensed core (a = 0.7, β = 4, t = 3 × 105). Left: measured occupation µv against the reversible prediction wvWv of Eq. (4) (both normalized); the dashed line is µv = wvWv. Right: occupation of the most visited vertex at each depth, showing the core droplet peaked a few levels below the root.

Figure 3: The branching-number law (11). Left: measured lines βc(a, b) for b = 2, 3, 4, 5 (from νR = 1/2), which fan out with b. Middle: the same divided by b −1; the four lines collapse, confirming βc ∝b −1 (see Table 1 for the quantitative version with confidence intervals). Right: the occupancy scale ¯m(a) = ((b−1)/βc)1/a, which is b-independent and increases with a.

Figure 4: Observation-time analysis at a = 0.6, b = 2, to t = 3 × 107 (24 realizations). Left: mean range R(t); the range grows for every β, linearly below βc and very slowly above (the ∝t0.1 guide is an effective-exponent reference; held-out extrapolation favours logarithmic growth). Middle: local exponent νR(t); it tends to 1 below βc and to a small value ≈0.1 above, without reaching zero. Right: the νR = 1/2 crossing βc(tmax), showing no systematic drift across the accessible decades (scatter of order 0.1).

Figure 5: Occupancy statistics at a = 0.6, b = 2, with t from 105 to 107. From left: ensemble mean ⟨m1⟩; Binder cumulant U, which tends to 2/3 in the condensed phase and dips negative on the spreading side; susceptibility χ = t Var(m1), whose peak near β ≈1.5 grows with t; and the distribution of m1 at t = 107, a spike at m1 ≈0 coexisting with a broad condensed lobe. The signatures are of a coexistence-type crossover; we do not claim a proven first-order transition.
